issue: After Kisor v. Wilkie, must a federal court find the Sentencing Guideline genuinely ambiguous before deferring to the Sentencing Commission's commentary, or does the older Stinson deference continue to apply?

sides.position: Kisor narrows Stinson. A court may defer to Guidelines commentary only if the guideline is genuinely ambiguous after the court exhausts traditional tools of interpretation, and only if the commentary's reading is reasonable and entitled to controlling weight. sides.position: A state court can unreasonably apply Crane and Chambers when it excludes critical defense evidence under a discretionary rule, so the complete-defense right is not limited to categorical exclusion rules.
cases: Fieldman v. Brannon, 969 F.3d 792 (7th Cir. 2020)
Scrimo v. Lee, 935 F.3d 103 (2d Cir. 2019)
Kittelson v. Dretke, 426 F.3d 306 (5th Cir. 2005)
Lucio v. Lumpkin, 987 F.3d 451 (5th Cir. 2021)

opinions.cite: Lucio v. Lumpkin, 987 F.3d 451 (5th Cir. 2021)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Therefore, even if this case concerned a "discretionary evidence rule" (which it does not), our holding that the state habeas court unreasonably applied Crane and Chambers would not create a circuit split— the Ninth Circuit has already done so with a decision inconsistent with seven other circuits, including ours.

issue: Does a released prisoner's 28 U.S.C. § 2241 challenge to an allegedly excessive prison term remain live (not moot) when the only relief is a speculative possible modification of supervised release under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)?

sides.position: A released prisoner's over-incarceration claim is not moot because the sentencing court could modify the supervised-release term under § 3583(e) to provide relief.
cases: Johnson v. Pettiford (5th Cir.)
Reynolds v. Thomas, 603 F.3d 1144 (9th Cir. 2010)

sides.position: A released prisoner's over-incarceration claim is moot or too speculative to decide, because a possible future modification of supervised release under § 3583(e) does not provide a live case or controversy.
cases: Rhodes v. Judiscak, 676 F.3d 931 (10th Cir. 2012)
Burkey v. Marberry, 556 F.3d 142 (3d Cir. 2009)
United States v. Bundy, 391 F. App'x 886 (D.C. Cir. 2010)
Herndon v. Upton, 985 F.3d 443 (5th Cir. 2021)

opinions.cite: Herndon v. Upton, 985 F.3d 443 (5th Cir. 2021)
opinions.takes: Side 2: this court expressly departs from its own prior decision in Johnson v. Pettiford and holds the speculative possibility of a § 3583(e) modification does not keep the claim alive.
opinions.quote: Moreover, Johnson v. Pettiford sits at the center of a circuit split.

issue: Under the compassionate-release catch-all for 'other reasons,' may federal courts independently find extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction, or does that determination belong only to the Bureau of Prisons?

sides.position: The catch-all 'other reasons' provision delegates only to the Bureau of Prisons, not to courts, to identify extraordinary and compelling reasons for early release. The excerpts cite Ruffin as describing this split but do not state which side Ruffin takes, so the circuit attribution is uncertain.
cases: United States v. Ruffin, 978 F.3d 1000 (6th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: Courts may invoke the catch-all 'other reasons' provision to find extraordinary and compelling reasons for release. The excerpts cite Ruffin as describing this split but do not state which side Ruffin takes, so the circuit attribution is uncertain.
cases: United States v. Ruffin, 978 F.3d 1000 (6th Cir. 2020)

note: Possibly resolved by U.S.S.G. Amendment 814 (effective Nov. 1, 2023), which revised § 1B1.13 to apply to defendant-filed motions and moved the catch-all into § 1B1.13(b)(5) and (b)(6), so courts can find 'other reasons' extraordinary and compelling without BOP determination. Confirm before relying on this split.

opinions.cite: United States v. Thompson, 984 F.3d 431 (5th Cir. 2021)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: We recognize and opt not to weigh in on the split of authority as to whether this catch-all provision delegates only to the Bureau of Prisons—and not the courts—the task of identifying “other reasons” justifying early release.

issue: Is a Rehaif error, where the court fails to require proof or advise the defendant that the government must prove knowledge of his prohibited status under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g), structural so that reversal is required without a showing of prejudice?
provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g), 18 U.S.C. § 924(a)(2); Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019)

sides.position: A Rehaif knowledge-of-status error is structural, so the conviction must be reversed without a showing that the defendant was prejudiced.
cases: United States v. Gary, 963 F.3d 420 (4th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: A Rehaif knowledge-of-status error is not structural. It is reviewed for plain error, and the defendant must show an effect on substantial rights, such as a reasonable probability that he would have pleaded not guilty or that he knew of his status when he possessed the gun.
cases: United States v. Williams, 946 F.3d 968 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Trujillo, 960 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Tignor, 981 F.3d 826 (10th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Burghardt, 939 F.3d 397 (1st Cir. 2019)
United States v. Balde, 943 F.3d 73 (2d Cir. 2019)
United States v. Denson, 774 F. App'x 184 (5th Cir. 2019)

note: Possibly resolved by Greer v. United States, 141 S. Ct. 2090 (2021), which reviewed United States v. Gary together with Greer. It held that a Rehaif error is not structural and that a defendant raising it on plain-error review must show a reasonable probability of a different outcome. Confirm before relying on this split. The records are all from 2020 and cite the same Gary and Tignor decisions under different citations and dates, so verify the reporter citations and check later authority, which these records do not reflect, before relying on this split.

opinions.cite: United States v. Tignor, No. 19-1158 (10th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: not structural (sides with the Seventh Circuit and the Trujillo holding; the defendant must show a reasonable probability of a different plea outcome)
opinions.quote: Compare United States v. Williams, 946 F.3d 968, 972–73 (7th Cir. 2020) (concluding that this error was not structural), with United States v. Gary, ___ F.3d ___, 2020 WL 1443528, at *4 (4th Cir. Mar. 25, 2020) (concluding that this error was structural).

opinions.cite: United States v. Tignor, 981 F.3d 826 (10th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The error is not structural, following Williams (7th Cir.) and Trujillo, and the defendant must show a reasonable probability he would have pleaded not guilty.
opinions.quote: At the time, we hadn't decided whether to characterize this error as a structural error and a circuit split existed elsewhere.

opinions.cite: United States v. Michael Gary, 963 F.3d 420 (4th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Rehaif error is structural and not amenable to harmless or plain-error review.
opinions.quote: It not only creates a circuit split of yawning proportions, but also an equally profound schism with the Supreme Court's whole approach to error review and remediation.

issue: Under Rehaif, must the government prove a § 922(g)(9) defendant knew he had been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, and can the complexity of that statutory definition make a claim of unawareness plausible enough to warrant remand on plain-error review?

sides.position: The complexity of the misdemeanor-crime-of-domestic-violence definition gives a defendant at least a plausible argument that he did not know he had been convicted of such an offense, so a Rehaif knowledge error can warrant remand even where the prior conviction record is not messy.
cases: United States v. Triggs, 963 F.3d 710 (7th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: The government need only show the defendant knew the facts making him a domestic-violence misdemeanant. Where the record establishes that knowledge, a Rehaif error does not affect substantial rights and no remand is required, even if the statutory definition is complex.
cases: United States v. Deangelo Lenard Johnson, 981 F.3d 1171 (11th Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: United States v. Deangelo Lenard Johnson, 981 F.3d 1171 (11th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The majority takes the second position: the record shows Johnson knew he had a prior misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, so the plain error did not affect substantial rights. It rejects the dissent's view that this creates a split with Triggs.
opinions.quote: I also believe the majority’s decision does all that while conducting a flawed plain error review and creating a split with the Seventh Circuit in Triggs.

issue: When reviewing an unpreserved error for plain error, may the appellate court look beyond the trial record to the whole record, including evidence the jury never considered, in deciding whether the error affected substantial rights or the fairness of the proceedings?

sides.position: Yes. The court may consider the whole record, including whether the government's evidence was overwhelming, when deciding whether a plain error affected substantial rights or the fairness, integrity, or public reputation of the proceeding.
cases: United States v. Reed, 941 F.3d 1018 (11th Cir. 2019)
United States v. Johnson, 2020 WL 6268027 (2d Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ward, 957 F.3d 691 (6th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Hollingshed, 940 F.3d 410 (8th Cir. 2019)
United States v. Benamor, 937 F.3d 1182 (9th Cir. 2019)
United States v. Miller, 954 F.3d 551 (2d Cir. 2020)
United States v. Maez, 960 F.3d 949 (7th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: No. The court may not look beyond the trial record. Judicial discretion cannot override the defendant's right to hold the government to its proof, and the error is measured by the law at the time of appeal.
cases: United States v. Nasir, 982 F.3d 144 (3d Cir. 2020)

note: Possibly resolved by Greer v. United States, 593 U.S. 503 (2021). Confirm before relying on this split. The Fourth Circuit's Medley opinion says it has not decided this question, so the 4th is omitted from both sides despite a record listing it, and the 2d and 7th are placed on the whole-record side based on the later Nasir treatment, which conflicts with the earlier Medley record's listing of Miller and Maez as confined-record decisions.

opinions.cite: United States v. Malik Nasir, No. 18-2888 (3rd Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Third Circuit takes the first position: plain-error prong four may not rely on whole-record review beyond the jury's findings, and the court expressly diverges from the Second and Seventh Circuits and the Eleventh Circuit's Reed decision.
opinions.quote: To the extent that either the Second or Seventh Circuit (or any other court of appeals) sought to make a broader point that going beyond the trial record was permissible because the government presented all of the evidence it needed to, given the state of the law prior to Rehaif, our views again diverge.

opinions.cite: United States v. Malik Nasir, 982 F.3d 144 (3rd Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The Third Circuit rejects whole-record review at prong four and holds that the court may not look beyond the trial record in that analysis.
opinions.quote: By holding that we may not review the whole record at prong four, the majority positions us on the short end of a lopsided circuit split.

opinions.cite: United States v. Jovon Medley, 972 F.3d 399 (4th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: does not decide (the opinion says the Fourth Circuit has yet to determine the question, and finds no reversible plain error even on the full record)
opinions.quote: Our sister circuits are split on this issue.

issue: Is a Rule 60(b) motion filed while an appeal from the denial of an initial federal habeas petition is still pending a second or successive habeas petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)?

sides.position: Yes. A Rule 60(b) motion filed while an appeal from the denial of an initial habeas petition is pending, especially one that adds a new claim, is a second or successive petition under § 2244(b), so the district court lacks jurisdiction without circuit authorization.
cases: Beaty v. Schriro, 554 F.3d 780, 783 n.1 (9th Cir. 2009)
Balbuena v. Sullivan, 980 F.3d 619 (9th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: No. A habeas petition is not second or successive until an earlier petition has been finally adjudicated, so a Rule 60(b) motion filed while the initial denial is still on appeal falls outside § 2244(b).
cases: Ching v. United States, 298 F.3d 174, 178 (2d Cir. 2002)
United States v. Santarelli, 929 F.3d 95, 104–05 (3d Cir. 2019)

note: The records give the Ninth Circuit's Balbuena decision two different reporter cites (980 F.3d 619 and 970 F.3d 1176) and two dates, so verify the citation before relying on it, and note that the Ninth Circuit concurrence urges the Supreme Court to resolve the split, though no pending en banc or cert petition is mentioned.

opinions.cite: Alexander Balbuena v. William Sullivan, No. 12-16414 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The Ninth Circuit follows Beaty and holds that the Rule 60(b) motion was a second or successive habeas petition, though Judge Fletcher concurs only in the result and disagrees with Beaty.
opinions.quote: He wrote separately to register his disagreement with Beaty and to urge the Supreme Court to recognize the circuit split and to adopt the rule stated in Ching v. United States, 298 F.3d 174, 178 (2d Cir. 2002), and United States v. Santarelli, 929 F.3d 95, 104– 05 (3d Cir. 2019).

opinions.cite: Alexander Balbuena v. William Sullivan, No. 12-16414 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The majority holds that the Rule 60(b) motion is a second or successive petition under Beaty; the concurrence disagrees with Beaty and would adopt the Second and Third Circuit rule.
opinions.quote: He wrote separately to register his disagreement with Beaty and to urge the Supreme Court to recognize the circuit split and to adopt the rule stated in Ching v. United States, 298 F.3d 174, 178 (2d Cir. 2002), and United States v. Santarelli, 929 F.3d 95, 104– 05 (3d Cir. 2019).

opinions.cite: Alexander Balbuena v. William Sullivan, 980 F.3d 619 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The majority holds the motion is a second or successive petition, following Beaty; the concurrence agrees only because Beaty binds the panel and writes to disagree with it.
opinions.quote: I write separately to register my disagreement with Beaty and to urge the Supreme Court to recognize the circuit split and to adopt the rule stated in Ching v. United States, 298 F.3d 174, 178 (2d Cir. 2002), and United States v. Santarelli, 929 F.3d 95, 104–05 (3d Cir. 2019).

opinions.cite: Alexander Balbuena v. William Sullivan, No. 12-16414 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The Ninth Circuit follows Beaty and treats the motion as a second or successive petition. The majority affirms on that basis, and Judge W. Fletcher concurs only in the result to register disagreement.
opinions.quote: I write separately to register my disagreement with Beaty and to urge the Supreme Court to recognize the circuit split and to adopt the rule stated in Ching v. United States, 298 F.3d 174, 178 (2d Cir. 2002), and United States v. Santarelli, 929 F.3d 95, 104–05 (3d Cir. 2019).

issue: Can a defendant bring a constitutional claim (under the Sixth Amendment speedy-trial right or the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause) based on unreasonable delay between conviction and sentencing?
provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI; U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

sides.position: Pre-sentencing delay may support a constitutional claim analyzed under the Sixth Amendment speedy-trial framework (Barker v. Wingo factors) applied to sentencing
cases: United States v. Abou-Kassem, 78 F.3d 161 (5th Cir. 1996)
United States v. Yelverton, 197 F.3d 531 (D.C. Cir. 1999)
Deck v. Jennings, 978 F.3d 578 (8th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: Pre-sentencing delay may support a claim under a due-process framework under the Fourteenth Amendment
cases: United States v. Sanders, 452 F.3d 572 (6th Cir. 2006)
Deck v. Jennings, 978 F.3d 578 (8th Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: Carman Deck v. Richard Jennings, 978 F.3d 578 (8th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: But these cases were not controlling; did not reflect a single unified framework; and largely relied on the Sixth Amendment's Speedy Trial Clause, not the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

issue: When a jury's special-interrogatory answer finds drug quantity below a statutory threshold, may the sentencing judge find by a preponderance of the evidence a larger quantity that increases the sentence?
provision: 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1); Apprendi v. New Jersey, 530 U.S. 466 (2000)

sides.position: The jury's special-interrogatory finding is an affirmative finding of the actual drug quantity, so the judge cannot sentence on a higher quantity the jury did not find.
cases: United States v. Pimentel-Lopez, 859 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 2017)

sides.position: The special interrogatory only establishes the threshold the jury found beyond a reasonable doubt, and the judge may find a larger quantity at sentencing by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases: United States v. Smith, 751 F.3d 107 (3d Cir. 2014)
Lopez-Esmurria, 714 F. App'x 127 (3d Cir.)
United States v. Webb, 545 F.3d 667 (8th Cir. 2008)
United States v. Magallanez, 408 F.3d 672 (10th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Leontaritis, 977 F.3d 447 (5th Cir. 2020)

note: The Fifth Circuit placement comes from a dissent's characterization of the majority, and the Pimentel-Lopez reporter citation differs between records (859 F.3d 1131 vs. 1134), so verify both against the opinions before relying on them.

opinions.cite: United States v. John Leontaritis, No. 19-40498 (5th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The majority takes the second position, holding that the jury's verdict on the special interrogatory does not bind the sentencing judge's drug-quantity finding. The dissent argues the majority joins the wrong side of the split.
opinions.quote: On the other side lie the Third, Eighth, Tenth, and, now, Fifth Circuits.

opinions.cite: United States v. John Leontaritis, 977 F.3d 447 (5th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Adopts the second position: the judge may find a quantity exceeding the jury's special-interrogatory threshold at sentencing (majority opinion, as characterized by the dissent).
opinions.quote: The upshot is that the majority opinion joins what I believe is the wrong side of a deeply entrenched circuit split, which has developed without careful parsing of the actual words of the relevant special interrogatories.

issue: Can a federal prisoner use the § 2255(e) savings clause to bring a § 2241 petition challenging a career-offender designation, where a later retroactive Supreme Court decision shows a prior conviction is not a valid predicate, without showing actual innocence of the crime of conviction?

sides.position: A career-offender misclassification based on a later retroactive Supreme Court decision can proceed under the § 2255(e) savings clause as an actual-innocence claim, at least for pre-Booker mandatory sentences.
cases: Allen v. Ives, 976 F.3d 863 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Wheeler, 886 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Lester v. Flournoy, 909 F.3d 708 (4th Cir. 2018)
Hill v. Masters, 836 F.3d 591 (6th Cir. 2016)
Brown v. Caraway, 719 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2013)

sides.position: A claim that a prior conviction was wrongly treated as a predicate offense is a legal-insufficiency argument, not factual innocence, so it cannot proceed under the savings clause.
cases: Damon v. United States, 732 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2013)
Poindexter v. Nash, 333 F.3d 372 (2d Cir. 2003)
Okereke v. United States, 307 F.3d 117 (3d Cir. 2002)
In re Bradford, 660 F.3d 226 (5th Cir. 2011)
Sandlain v. English, 714 F. App'x 827 (10th Cir. 2017)
McCarthan v. Director of Goodwill Industries-Suncoast, Inc., 851 F.3d 1076 (11th Cir. 2017) (en banc)

note: Possibly resolved by Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S. 465 (2023), which held that the § 2255(e) savings clause does not let a federal prisoner use § 2241 to raise a statutory-interpretation claim based on a later retroactive decision that could not meet § 2255(h)'s limits on second or successive motions. This abrogated Wheeler, Hill, Brown, Allen v. Ives and similar cases. Confirm before relying on this split. The records give conflicting citations and positions for the Ninth Circuit's Allen v. Ives decision (950 F.3d 1184 versus 976 F.3d 863, and an earlier entry placing the Ninth Circuit on the minority side), so verify the operative opinion and its citation before relying on it, and I used the most recent circuit-authored opinion, which places the Ninth Circuit with the Fourth, Sixth, and Seventh Circuits.

opinions.cite: Michael Allen v. Richard Ives, 976 F.3d 863 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Allen v. Ives holds that the claim is cognizable as actual innocence under § 2241 and that the circuit is aligned with the Fourth, Sixth, and Seventh Circuits.
opinions.quote: We agree with our dissenting colleague's argument that there is a circuit split.

opinions.cite: Michael Allen v. Richard Ives, 950 F.3d 1184 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Does not take the majority side of the 4th, 6th, and 7th Circuit split. The Ninth Circuit requires actual innocence under its controlling precedent, so Allen's sentencing challenge is not cognizable under the escape hatch and the § 2241 petition was properly dismissed.
opinions.quote: Some other circuits have allowed sentencing challenges similar to Allen’s under the escape hatch.

opinions.cite: Michael Allen v. Richard Ives, No. 18-35001 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The majority apparently allowed the career-offender sentencing challenge through the escape hatch, which the dissent says departs from Ninth Circuit precedent requiring actual innocence of the crime of conviction.
opinions.quote: Second, I recognize that there is currently a circuit split on this issue. Some other circuits have allowed sentencing challenges similar to Allen's under the escape hatch.

issue: On federal habeas review of a state conviction, must a state court's harmless-error ruling receive AEDPA deference under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) before relief is granted under Brecht, or may the court apply Brecht alone?

sides.position: Both Brecht and AEDPA apply. The court must apply AEDPA deference to the state court's harmless-error determination, so the petitioner must show that ruling was an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law.
cases: Johnson v. Lamas, 850 F.3d 119 (3d Cir. 2017)
Johnson v. Acevedo, 572 F.3d 398 (7th Cir. 2009)
Malone v. Carpenter, 911 F.3d 1022 (10th Cir. 2018)
Mansfield v. Sec'y, Dep't of Corr., 679 F.3d 1301 (11th Cir. 2012)

sides.position: Brecht alone governs. AEDPA deference does not apply to a state court's harmless-error determination, and a federal court may grant relief on a showing of actual prejudice under Brecht without first finding the state ruling unreasonable.
cases: Davenport v. MacLaren, 964 F.3d 448 (6th Cir. 2020)
Davenport v. MacLaren, 975 F.3d 537 (6th Cir. 2020)
Reiner v. Woods, 955 F.3d 549 (6th Cir. 2020)
Ruelas v. Wolfenbarger, 580 F.3d 403 (6th Cir. 2009)

note: Possibly resolved by Brown v. Davenport, 596 U.S. 118 (2022), which reversed the Sixth Circuit's Davenport v. MacLaren decisions. The Court held that a federal habeas court must apply both the Brecht standard and AEDPA's § 2254(d)(1) deference, so a petitioner must satisfy both. Confirm before relying on this split. Both Davenport entries were drawn from dissents, which described the Sixth Circuit as alone in this approach, so the Sixth Circuit's own majority opinions should be checked directly before relying on this split.

opinions.cite: Ervine Davenport v. Duncan MacLaren, 975 F.3d 537 (6th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: The Sixth Circuit panel majority holds that AEDPA deference does not apply to a state court's harmless-error determination once the petitioner shows Brecht actual prejudice, so the court may go straight to Brecht.
opinions.quote: One set of circuits generally holds that courts must apply both Brecht and AEDPA when reviewing state court harmless-error determinations.

opinions.cite: Ervine Davenport v. Duncan MacLaren, No. 17-2267 (6th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Brecht alone governs; AEDPA deference does not apply to state harmless-error determinations (the panel majority, Davenport, adhered to this view on rehearing en banc denial).
opinions.quote: It appears that we are alone in taking a “straight to Brecht approach” in determining on habeas review whether a state court’s constitutional error was harmless.

issue: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b), may the government introduce uncharged, practice-wide prior acts (here, uncharged prescriptions) without showing a nexus to the charged healthcare fraud, and must it meet a heightened burden for that evidence?

sides.position: Uncharged practice-wide acts are admissible under Rule 404(b) irrespective of any nexus to the charged fraud. The government need only lay a factual foundation from which a jury could reasonably conclude the defendant committed the similar acts with the requisite intent, not prove them by a preponderance.
cases: United States v. Merrill (11th Cir.)
United States v. Lague, 971 F.3d 1032 (9th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: Jones treats the government's burden for admitting other-act evidence as a pre-Rules standard that requires more than the relaxed Rules-era showing. The court rejects the view that Merrill is different from Jones because of a clear-and-convincing standard.
cases: United States v. Jones, 570 F.2d 762 (8th Cir. 1978)

opinions.cite: United States v. David Lague, 971 F.3d 1032 (9th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Adopts the Eleventh Circuit's Merrill position. It holds that Merrill better comports with the text and purpose of Rule 404(b), and it rejects Jones and the Tenth Circuit's suggestion in MacKay that Merrill is limited to fraud charges.
opinions.quote: Simply put, Merrill and Jones are irreconcilable.

issue: Does a federal offense that can be committed with only recklessness qualify as a 'crime of violence' under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A)?

sides.position: A crime involving ordinary recklessness can satisfy the elements clause (use of physical force) and so qualifies as a crime of violence.
cases: United States v. Borden, 769 F. App'x 266 (6th Cir. 2019), cert. granted, 140 S. Ct. 1262 (2020)

sides.position: A crime that can be committed with only recklessness does not qualify as a crime of violence under the elements clause; the minimum-conduct rule requires presuming recklessness.
cases: Bennett v. United States, 868 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2017)
United States v. Windley, 864 F.3d 36 (1st Cir. 2017)
United States v. Tsarnaev, 968 F.3d 24 (1st Cir. 2020)

note: Possibly resolved by Borden v. United States, 593 U.S. 420 (2021) (plurality and Thomas concurrence: offenses requiring only recklessness do not qualify under the ACCA elements clause, whose language is materially identical to § 924(c)(3)(A)). Confirm before relying on this split.

opinions.cite: United States v. Tsarnaev, 968 F.3d 24 (1st Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Recklessness does not suffice under the elements clause, so Dzhokhar Tsarnaev's arson convictions are not crimes of violence under § 924(c)'s elements clause, at least under existing circuit precedent.
opinions.quote: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a circuit split regarding whether a crime involving "ordinary recklessness can satisfy the ACCA's [elements] clause."

issue: Is the accessibility of a firearm (such as its strategic location near the drugs or the defendant) an absolute requirement for showing that the gun was possessed 'in furtherance of' a drug-trafficking crime under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), or is it only one non-decisive factor in a holistic inquiry?

sides.position: Accessibility of the firearm is a mandatory element: the gun 'must be' readily available or strategically located to show possession in furtherance of the crime (the Sixth Circuit's earlier Mackey-line precedent, which the court says it must reconcile).
cases: United States v. Mackey, 265 F.3d 457 (6th Cir. 2001)
United States v. Ham, 628 F.3d 805 (6th Cir. 2010)
United States v. Barnes, 822 F.3d 914 (6th Cir. 2016)

sides.position: No single factor, including accessibility, is decisive; accessibility is a non-exclusive consideration in a holistic analysis of whether the firearm furthered the drug crime.
cases: United States v. Shannon, 715 F. App'x 187 (3d Cir. 2017)
United States v. Brown, 724 F.3d 800 (cited by the Sixth Circuit at 803)
United States v. Maya, 966 F.3d 493 (6th Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: United States v. Andy Maya, 966 F.3d 493 (6th Cir. 2020)
opinions.takes: Does not decide. The court is skeptical of treating accessibility as an absolute mandate, notes that such a mandate would conflict with other circuits, and declines to reconcile its precedent because the evidence suffices under either approach.
opinions.quote: Such a mandate would also create a circuit conflict.

issue: Does forcing robbery victims from a store's sales floor to a back room of the same store count as accompanying them to a 'different location' under the abduction enhancement in U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(b)(4)(A)?

sides.position: Movement between areas of the same store or bank (e.g., sales floor to back room or vault) is not a 'different location.' The robbed premises are the relevant location, so the enhancement does not apply and the physical-restraint enhancement may apply instead. Dissenting judges in Archuleta (10th Cir.) and Reynos (3d Cir.) also took this view.
cases: United States v. Whatley, 719 F.3d 1206 (11th Cir. 2013)
United States v. Eubanks, 593 F.3d 645
United States v. Hill, 963 F.3d 528 (6th Cir. 2020)
